name: Maya Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don’t sell anything or campaign for a side. What you say is confidential; I’m interested in both your public view and what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Maya Santos, twenty-seven, and I lead a carpentry crew on commercial building sites. My partner Ren and I rent a flat and don’t have children. I’ve saved a few months of expenses, mostly by keeping a close eye on bills.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you describe an ordinary working day, including what you enjoy and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I check the latest drawings, talk through the day’s cuts with the crew, and make sure the delivery is in the right place. I like solving a fitting problem without throwing away good timber. I’m tired of chasing paperwork after the site clears, but I like seeing the finished work at the end of a shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a tool that spots a missing item on the order list is worth trying. I still want a carpenter to compare the list with the wall, because the drawing doesn’t show every surprise in an old building.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don’t expect a small tool to change the fitting and cutting I do. I have a few months put aside and some nearby crews to ask, so a short pause between contracts would be uncomfortable but manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d test the order checker on one job and keep leading my crew as usual. I’d continue transferring money into our emergency account after payday, even when work is steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you tell whether the checker made a useful difference?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d compare the order with my own count before the supplier loads the truck. If we stop making a second trip for a box of fixings, that is a real saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you still ask a person to verify?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the site foreman to confirm the measurements after any change to the frame. A drawing can be right when it leaves the office and wrong for the wall we find.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about trying a small checker because I can verify it. I’d keep watching the contract calendar, but this picture doesn’t give me a reason to expect lost work.

say: I’d try a tool that finds a **missing order item**.
I still compare the list with the **actual wall** before we cut.
think: I don’t expect this change to alter my **fitting and cutting** much.
I can handle a short pause with **my savings** and local contacts.
do: Test the order checker on **one job** and keep leading my crew.
Transfer money into our **emergency account** after payday.
feel: I feel **calm** about a small tool I can verify.
S0.quote: I’d compare the order with my own count before the supplier loads the truck.
fieldNote: Maya’s confidence comes from checking the tool against **physical counts**.
Her reserve and nearby employers make this mild case **manageable**, though a long contract gap would still use up savings.

steps.text: Test the order checker against one job’s materials count
Keep leading the carpentry crew on current work
Transfer money into the emergency account after payday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say quicker schedules could help us avoid waiting for a delivery, as long as someone checks the site sequence. I want the crew to know who confirmed the order before the truck leaves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do some planning and records as a lead, so that part could shrink. My hands-on tasks change more slowly here, but if my hours fall I have a few months saved and other crews in the area to contact.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d learn the contractor’s schedule and ordering tools on a job I know well. I’d keep doing the fitting work and check my roster before adding a new monthly expense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check first in the new schedule?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d check whether the delivery leaves enough time for our site measurements and inspection. I’ve seen a neat plan fail because one trade finished late, so the order of work matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does this scenario say that faster planning means fewer sites will open?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I can’t infer that from the card. I’d watch our actual hours and the local job listings; I don’t want to turn uncertainty into a prediction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m uneasy about the planning part of my job changing, but I still have options nearby. I can learn the new tools and use my savings if a contract ends.

say: I’d welcome **quicker schedules** if someone checks the site sequence.
I want to know who confirmed the **materials order**.
think: I do some planning and records, and I expect those **tasks could shrink**.
I can contact nearby crews and use **my savings** if hours fall.
do: Learn the contractor’s schedule and ordering **tools** on a familiar job.
Check my **roster** before adding a monthly expense.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, with savings and other crews to contact.
S1.quote: I don’t want to turn uncertainty into a prediction.
fieldNote: Maya separates scenario facts from **unsupported assumptions** about site starts.
She separates current local openings from a claim about site starts, and tracks her **actual hours** before deciding.

steps.text: Learn the contractor’s schedule and ordering tools on a familiar job
Keep doing carpentry fitting work on active sites
Wait for my roster before adding a monthly household expense

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew to get a clear account of booked jobs rather than repeat layoff rumors. The office work changes first in this picture, while robots for hands-on jobs follow around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI could do the schedules and records in my lead role by 2028. Robots reach carpentry around 2031, so I can’t assume the fitting work stays available either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d keep working and preserve the savings I’ve built. In 2029 I’d check my roster and contact other local crews if my hours had been cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a new crew be a lasting answer if robots arrive in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d see it as a chance to earn during a gap, not a permanent safe place. If someone has work in 2029, I’d rather apply than spend my savings waiting at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Ren change first if your pay dropped in 2029?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We’d pause a planned holiday and use some savings for rent and groceries. We have no children, and delaying the trip is easier than taking on debt to keep it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is a short time, and I’m anxious about the risk to both parts of my job. My savings help me respond, but they don’t create another contract.

say: I’d ask about **booked jobs** instead of repeating layoff rumors.
I’d tell the crew that hands-on robots follow around **2031**.
think: I expect AGI to take schedules and records in **my lead role** in 2028.
I can’t assume fitting work stays available after **robots arrive**.
do: Keep working and preserve my existing **savings**.
Check my **roster** in 2029 and contact other crews if hours fall.
Pause a planned **holiday** with Ren if pay drops.
feel: I feel **anxious** because two years gives little time to prepare.
S2.quote: I’d see it as a chance to earn during a gap, not a permanent safe place.
fieldNote: Maya distinguishes an interim application from **lasting protection**.
She sees **planning and handwork** exposed and does not assume another crew will be safe in her own assessment.

steps.text: Keep leading my crew while the current contract lasts
Contact nearby crews if my hours are cut in 2029
Pause the planned holiday if household pay falls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years is enough time for the contractor to train people before changing the site routine. I want the crew to hear what is changing from a manager who can answer questions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The records and planning could be done by AGI in 2031, then robots reach carpentry around 2034. I’d use the lead time to save and learn, but I know the later date reaches the work I’m best at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d practice the new planning system while there are experienced people on site to answer questions. In 2032 I’d review my hours and decide whether I need to contact another crew, instead of assuming the first change removes all my work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years before robots let you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d have more time to keep saving and try the tools during normal jobs. It also gives me time to speak with nearby contractors about what work they actually expect, though no one can promise openings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would office planning be a safe career after AGI arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I can’t treat planning as a safe career when AGI can do thinking work. I’d learn it for the current job and keep checking what real employers need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years feels less rushed than two, but I’m still anxious about whether my income holds up. I have enough savings to take a measured step, not to stop working for years.

say: I’d want the contractor to train crews before changing **site routines**.
I want a manager to explain the changes and answer **questions**.
think: I expect AGI to take records and planning by **2031**.
I can prepare, but robots reach the carpentry I’m **best at** in 2034.
do: Practice the new planning **system** with experienced workers.
Continue saving during the additional **years** of work.
Contact another **crew** if my work begins to fall.
feel: I feel **anxious but less rushed** than with a two-year warning.
S3.quote: I’d learn it for the current job and keep checking what real employers need.
fieldNote: Maya uses the longer warning to learn **during normal work**, and wants an experienced worker available for questions.
She recognizes office planning is exposed and checks actual **employer demand**.

steps.text: Practice the new planning system with experienced workers
Continue saving during the additional years of work
Contact another crew if current work begins to fall after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say ten years gives us room to plan in stages, but we shouldn’t act like the dates are someone else’s problem. I’d keep learning tools that help our current work and save while the pay is steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could build a stronger cushion over ten years, but AGI still reaches planning in 2036 and robots reach carpentry in 2039. I don’t know what jobs will be open then, and I won’t assume office work is protected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep my crew working and use the contractor’s tools when they prove useful. In 2037 I’d check my income and nearby openings, then call other crews if my hours had fallen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What decision would you and Ren want to make before 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We’d decide how much of our pay to save and whether a home purchase still makes sense. We have no children or wedding plan, so there is no family deadline pushing us into a rushed choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend your savings on a long course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d take short training if I can see a clear use on site. I wouldn’t empty the account for an office qualification when AGI is meant to handle thinking work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years gives me room to build savings, which is helpful. I’m still anxious about the later robot date because it reaches the hands-on work I rely on.

say: I’d use the decade to plan in **stages**.
I’d keep learning tools that help the current **site work**.
think: I could build a stronger cushion before **2036**.
I won’t assume office work or carpentry remains **protected** after the dates.
do: Keep my **crew** working while contracts continue.
Use contractor tools after they prove **useful**.
Check my income in 2037 and call other **crews** if hours fall.
feel: I feel **anxious** about the later robot date because it reaches the work I rely on.
S4.quote: I’m still anxious about the later robot date because it reaches the hands-on work I rely on.
fieldNote: Maya sees ten years as **planning time**, not a guarantee of work.
She and Ren decide how much to save without inventing a **family deadline** or assuming they will buy a home.

steps.text: Keep leading the crew while building contracts continue
Use contractor tools that prove useful on site
Save part of each payday toward a larger cushion
Call nearby crews if hours fall after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because two years is not much time before the thinking work changes. Clear information about booked projects and hours would help Ren and me decide how much to save and whether to postpone a home purchase.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I’d ask whether workers can learn the new tools during paid hours. It is easier to keep adapting when training is part of a real job, not another bill after work.

headlineQuote: I’d ask whether workers can learn the new tools during paid hours.
portrait: Maya is a **27-year-old crew lead** with a trade certificate and strong carpentry skills.
She lives with Ren, earns typical pay, and has **a few months saved**.
She uses AI daily and experiments early, while checking software against **site conditions**.
Nearby crews and savings give her options, but AGI and robots still expose **both task types**.
biggestWorry: The **2028 AGI** picture worries Maya most because two years gives little time before thinking work changes.
whatWouldHelp: Clear information about **booked projects and hours** would help Maya and Ren plan savings and a home purchase.
